Shipwreck
ship'rek
n. and v. (the destruction of a vessel; in 1 Timothy, the ruin made of faith by a discarded conscience)
From ship and wreck, rendering the Greek nauageo — from naus (ship) and agnumi (to break) — to suffer the breaking of a vessel. Paul uses it once of the sea and once of the soul.

Biblical Definition

Paul knew the literal thing three times over: “Thrice was I beaten with rods, once was I stoned, thrice I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I have been in the deep” (2 Corinthians 11:25). He then takes the word and does something far more sobering with it. Charging Timothy to war a good warfare (1 Timothy 1:18), he adds the terms: “Holding faith, and a good conscience; which some having put away concerning faith have made shipwreck” (1 Timothy 1:19). The order in that sentence is the whole doctrine. What was put away was the good conscience; what was wrecked was the faith. Men do not usually reason their way out of Christianity and then begin to sin; they sin, refuse to repent, silence the conscience that accuses them, and afterwards find reasons why the faith was never true. The conscience is the ballast, and a ship that throws its ballast overboard will founder in the first heavy sea. Paul names two who did it — “Of whom is Hymenaeus and Alexander; whom I have delivered unto Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Timothy 1:20) — and even that severity has a remedial end.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines shipwreck as the destruction of a ship by rocks, shoals or tempest, and figuratively the destruction or ruin of anything.

expand to see more

SHIPWRECK, n. The destruction of a ship or vessel by being cast ashore or broken to pieces by beating against rocks and the like.

2. The parts of a shattered ship.

3. Destruction; ruin; as the shipwreck of a fortune.

SHIPWRECK, v.t. To destroy by running ashore or on rocks or sand-banks.

CONSCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge, or judgment of right and wrong; the faculty by which we judge of the moral rectitude of our own actions.

Key Scripture

1 Timothy 1:19 — "Holding faith, and a good conscience; which some having put away concerning faith have made shipwreck:"

1 Timothy 1:20 — "Of whom is Hymenaeus and Alexander; whom I have delivered unto Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme."

1 Timothy 1:18 — "This charge I commit unto thee, son Timothy, according to the prophecies which went before on thee, that thou by them mightest war a good warfare;"

2 Corinthians 11:25 — "Thrice was I beaten with rods, once was I stoned, thrice I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I have been in the deep;"

Modern Corruption

Apostasy is explained as an intellectual conclusion honestly reached, when Paul traces it to a conscience deliberately put away.

expand to see more

The public account of leaving the faith is almost always a story about evidence — the sufferer read, thought, and could no longer believe. Paul supplies a different order of causation and he supplies it as an apostle: the good conscience is put away first, and the wreck of faith follows. The verb is active and deliberate; it is what a man does, not what happens to him. This is not a claim that every doubt is disguised sin, and the honest struggles of believers should never be handled as though it were. It is a claim that the road out generally runs through an unrepented sin the conscience was ordered to stop mentioning.

The second corruption is a misuse of this verse against the doctrine of perseverance, as though shipwrecked faith proved that the elect may finally fall. Scripture holds both truths without strain: those whom God effectually calls He keeps, and a man may hold a profession, serve in a church, and be finally lost. The Confession states it exactly — perseverance is the fruit of regeneration, and its absence reveals what was never present. Hymenaeus and Alexander are a warning to the professing, not a threat to the regenerate, and the warnings themselves are among the means God uses to keep His own.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek nauageo (G3489), to suffer shipwreck — 1 Timothy 1:19, 2 Corinthians 11:25; apotheomai (G683), to thrust away — 1 Timothy 1:19.

expand to see more

Greek nauageo (G3489) — to be shipwrecked; only twice, once literally at 2 Corinthians 11:25 and once of the faith at 1 Timothy 1:19.

Greek apotheomai (G683) — to thrust away, to put from oneself; 1 Timothy 1:19, and the deliberate act that precedes the wreck.

Greek suneidesis (G4893) — conscience; a favourite word of the Pastorals, held together with faith in 1 Timothy 1:5, 1:19, 3:9.

Greek strateuomai (G4754) — to war, to serve as a soldier; 1 Timothy 1:18, the warfare whose terms verse 19 supplies.

1 Timothy 1:20 shows even excommunication aimed at recovery: that they may learn not to blaspheme.

Usage

"“Concerning faith have made shipwreck” — the vessel is the profession, and it can break up."

"“Holding faith, and a good conscience” — the second is the ballast of the first."

"The conscience goes overboard before the faith goes down."
